The largest such k is 2.

**Upper bound.** Each colour class must connect all V vertices, so it needs at least V − 1 edges. Hence k(V − 1) ≤ 2022.

A convex polyhedron has a planar graph, so E ≤ 3V − 6. With E = 2022 this gives V ≥ 676.

Then k ≤ 2022/675 < 3, so k ≤ 2.

**Construction for k = 2.** Take V = 676. Then E = 3V − 6 = 2022, so the polyhedron must be a triangulation.

The degree sum is 4044 = 6·664 + 5·12, so the degrees can be 5 and 6 only, with 664 vertices of degree 6 and 12 of degree 5. I did not construct such a triangulation explicitly. I am relying on the standard fact that triangulations with these degree sequences exist. The usual icosahedral-type families have V = 10T + 2 vertices, which does not give 676, so this existence step is assumed rather than verified.

Given such a triangulation, two edge-disjoint spanning trees exist because the graph is 3-connected with 3V − 6 edges. Two trees need only 2·675 = 1350 ≤ 2022 edges. Colour one tree with colour 1 and put all remaining edges in colour 2, which still contains the second spanning tree. Each colour then connects every pair of vertices.

ANSWER: 2
